she has about $124 a week to live on. We would need to take $30 from that to pay for
that person’s home care. That is what National is doing to the old people of Mana, and it
believes that those people will turn out to vote for it. I say that National members are
dreaming. They are in cloud-cuckoo-land.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: The cry has gone up—the cry has
gone up. Who is in charge over there? I think that probably the man who sits in the far
10 Nov 2010 General Debate 15171
corner of the House is in charge, the one with the texts from the person sitting in an
office in New York. He is the one in charge. It is very clear that there is no leadership
on that side of the House. I have been a whip. I know what it is like to have a split vote.
I do not believe that one would have a split vote on a closure motion—a split vote on a
closure motion, for heaven’s sake! Apart from the fact that Phil Goff seems to talk
about everything and know very little, there is no leadership in the Labour Party.
The fact is that we look at this list of a split vote and we see that we again have, as
my colleague said, the magic number of 17. Four Labour MPs came to this House and
did not have an opinion on a bill as critical as the Rugby World Cup 2011
(Empowering) Bill. One or two did not even bother turning up. I bet Chris Carter was
sitting in the back of the room. It is outrageous that we should see Labour in such a
mess that it has a split vote on a closure motion.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Tell the truth.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: The mad dog sitting in the corner there, who needs to take
his pills, wants to look at the truth. This is the truth. The list states that the Ayes were
23, the Noes were 11, four abstained, and two were missing. That is the truth, I say to
Mr Mallard. How a former Minister for the Rugby World Cup can abstain—abstain—
from voting on a bill that will ensure that the Rugby World Cup is a success is beyond
me.
While the Opposition is in disarray, this National Government is getting on with the
things that matter to New Zealand. Absolutely! The important things that matter to
this—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I apologise for interrupting the Minister during her speech; I will
stop the clock. The member will desist from that kind of totally objectionable
interjection. I mean what I say. He will desist.

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I agree with your
comment, but the difficulty that caused the reaction was a most unparliamentary
comment the Minister, whilst using the full microphone, made about my colleague. She
referred not only to a derogatory name but also to an action, and it was broadcast with
the full microphone on. My colleague did not have that benefit—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: We have interrupted the member’s speech. I heard what happened,
and it was in response to earlier very unsatisfactory interjections. But as to the last one,
I will not tolerate members interjecting about personal matters of members of this
House. I absolutely put my foot down on that. I apologise to the Minister for
interrupting her speech, but that will not be tolerated while I am Speaker.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I will take the opportunity this afternoon, whilst the
Opposition is in such disarray, to talk about what is happening in the rest of the world. I
recently attended a meeting of OECD Ministers of Education. It was amazing, when we
are in the middle of industrial negotiations with teacher unions, to realise what is
happening in the rest of the world and to realise how good we have it here under this
National-led Government. In Italy 42,000 teaching jobs are being lost—42,000. In
France next year 13,500 teaching jobs will go, and they are looking at losing 40,000-
odd teachers. In Russia they are talking about losing 200,000 teachers out of their
system in order to balance their education budgets—200,000 teachers. In Ireland there is
a 2-year pay freeze for public servants, which of course includes teachers. In England
they have just announced their Budget. There is growth of 0.1 percent in real terms each
year for the education budget in the next few years. That means that schools will have to
save about a billion dollars; they will have to make savings of around a billion dollars.
That is extraordinary, compared with this country, where we put a new $300 million
into education last year and the year before that. I read on a website today that schools
15172 General Debate 10 Nov 2010
in England will be forced to publish teachers’ salaries, qualifications, and sickness rates
in order to determine whether they offer value for money.
When we look at what the National Government is doing here in New Zealand, we
see that we are focused on lifting long-term economic growth, in which we know
education plays a key part. We want to make sure that all our children learn to read,
write, and do maths while they are in primary school. We want to make sure that every
child leaves school with a qualification that will enable them to succeed in this modern
world. We know that we had to rebalance our tax system. We know we need better,
smarter public services.

items.speaker: Hon DARREN HUGHES
items.text: If any member of the executive greeted with
great delight the announcement made by the Prime Minister this week that there will not
be a major Cabinet reshuffle before the general election, it would have been the Hon
Anne Tolley. I think her lack of passion in describing her education portfolio, at the tail
end of her speech, just shows why, when everyone thought the skids would be put under
her before the election, she must have been so happy at John Key’s announcement that
there would be no change in Cabinet. The national standards slogan that the Minister is
trying to turn into a policy is a disaster, up hill and down dale. Anybody who delves into
the issue to understand it gets to see that it was a slogan for an election; it was never
meant to be a policy for a country. That is what all the people tell us who sit in meetings
and look at the issue in a clever way—be they parents, students, or teachers. The same
thing comes through time and time again: the slogan does not work as a policy. But
then, of course, it is part of the whole mantra of “smile and wave”.
I want to follow on from what the deputy leader of the Labour Party, the Hon
Annette King, had to say about the Mana by-election. There are some really important
issues for that by-election, to be held on 20 November, that we believe are worth
exploring. Annette King has talked about the health issues in that electorate. I want to
touch on some of the transport issues in the Mana electorate.
At the last general election, residents of the Mana and Ōtaki electorates thought there
was a bipartisan transport policy between Labour and National when it came to
transport. They thought that both parties were saying the same thing. In fact, the
National candidates went quite some way to wrap themselves in the cloak of the Labour
Government of that time. They said they believed in Transmission Gully, and they said
they believed in the 90 percent Government subsidy for a local two-lane Western Link
Road, like the one that the Labour Party had proposed and funded. They said they
believed in the further electrification and double tracking of rail. Those were the things
they said at the time of the general election.
Then, about a year or so ago, in the dead of night, Steven Joyce, the Minister of
Transport, who runs large swathes of the Government behind closed doors, decided he
had a better idea than everybody else—a bit of a theme there, actually. He thought he
knew better than absolutely everybody else. He turned up and said he had lived in the
community 35 years ago, so therefore he knew what the answer should be. He said a
four-lane, 110 kilometre an hour motorway, an autobahn, should go right through the
whole of the Kapiti coast. That is what he said he was going to do, but that was not what
the National Party had campaigned on, and the community was taken by huge surprise
because of that.
Of course, during the consultation period the big, bold, decisive, brave, and
courageous National MPs in the area, when asked what their opinion was, said nothing.
They had no opinion on the preferred option in the consultation period. They had
absolutely nothing to say about it at all. They sat on the fence, waiting and waiting to
see what the Minister of Transport would decide. As soon as he made a decision, they
10 Nov 2010 General Debate 15173
were gung-ho behind him—the greatest cheerleaders ever to have walked along the
Kapiti coast. That is how bold and brave they were.
On Sunday this week the people of Kapiti were meant to find out where the
expressway will be going. The New Zealand Transport Agency spent $22,000 on
inviting people from all around the region to come and see the plans. As we heard in
question time yesterday and today, Steven Joyce, the Harry Potter equivalent of Lord
Voldemort in this Government, discovered that this issue would be coming up before
the by-election, and he decided—

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: Harry Potter saves the day.

items.speaker: Hon DARREN HUGHES
items.text: If only Tau Henare had gone to Hogwarts School of
Witchcraft and Wizardry, he might be in a better state than he is in. But he would join
any old organisation, which is why he is sitting over there on the National benches at
the present time. As soon as Steven Joyce found out that this issue was coming up too
close to the Mana by-election, he cancelled the consultation. On 2 November the
Government cancelled the consultation, due to take place on 7 November, until after the
Mana by-election.
Do members not think that the National MPs for the area would be outraged at this
disenfranchisement of the people of Kapiti? Do they not think the National MPs would
be waving around pieces of paper, saying that it was not good enough, and that there
comes a time when MPs have to put their community before their party, so they were
breaking ranks with their Government in order to make sure that their people had a say
before the by-election? But can members guess what? There was not a word, not a
complaint, not a criticism, and not a demand for a new series of dates. The National
MPs sat there boldly, saying absolutely nothing. They are lambs in Parliament and
lambs in the electorate. It is absolutely unbelievable. Now we know that these plans will
remain secret, because the Government is scared to release them to the Mana electorate.
It is a disgrace. Government members should be upfront with the public about the
situation. They should go back to Labour’s policy at the last election, which they said
they were in favour of, as well.

items.speaker: PAUL QUINN
items.text: I want to return to the theme that the mover of the
motion started with, and that is the chaos that currently prevails within the Labour
Party. We can have a look at one of the names that the Associate Minister and Leader of
the House mentioned—Charles Chauvel. I do not know whether members noticed, but
Charles was having a “Secret Squirrel” session with Chris Carter this afternoon, at the
back of the House. Perhaps Charles has decided that the mood for change has re-
emerged, and no doubt Charles wants to be at the front of the queue. Charles likes the
baubles of office; there is no question about that. He wants to be where the winner will
be. It is no wonder he was up there.
Grant Robertson spent most of the debate last night speaking against the motion. He
rose three or four times last night to speak against the motion. I looked at the list. What
does it show? It shows that he voted in favour of the motion. Grant cannot actually
make up his mind. He naturally, probably, belongs with the Chris Carter faction—the
17 faction—but he has obviously decided that currently, as he has moved up in the
ranks to the front of the 2008 fraternity, he clearly owes some patronage, some payback,
to the current leader. So he obviously decided in the end that he is making better grass
where he is at the moment. Clearly, though, he is ready to jump ship.
We then move to Iain Lees-Galloway. He spoke vigorously and regularly against the
bill, but he voted for it. I am not quite sure, but he clearly was a mirror image of Grant.
He is really in Phil’s camp, and unfortunately he got a bit betwixt and between. But that
is not unusual. He proceeded to tell us how the annual Rugby Sevens tournament should
be run, but he then admitted he had never been to one. But that is not unusual behaviour
15174 General Debate 10 Nov 2010
from Labour members. They spend most of their time lecturing people on things they
have never known and never experienced.
I come now to Trevor Mallard. Here is a guy who has fought this particular bill,
tooth and nail. He lost every battle—but I look at the voting sheet, and what has he
done? He has voted in favour. Why did he do that? I suspect that it is because he wants
to make sure that he gets invitations to the corporate box. He is a bit scared, and I know
for a fact that he has already had a conversation with the New Zealand Rugby Football
Union about getting free tickets to the Rugby World Cup. I know that for a fact. On the
one hand he wants to fight the bill but on the other hand he knows that if he does not
vote for it, the New Zealand Rugby Football Union will not give him tickets.
Shane Jones, my friend at the back, did not know what to do.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I know it was done in
humour, but I think there was some suggestion of motive—in this case, very expensive
motive—in my regard as to a vote yesterday. I want to place on the record that that is
not correct.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I hear the member. If the member with the floor had alleged that an
outside influence had influenced the member’s vote, that would definitely be an issue of
order. But I do not think he quite did that. He put it the other way around. He alleged
that the member was thinking about something, and I do not think that is out of order. A
point of order should not be used to interrupt the speaker.

items.speaker: PAUL QUINN
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I come now to Shane. Shane did not vote,
at all. He wanted a foot in both camps. Do members know why he wants a foot in both
camps?

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: He wasn’t here.

items.speaker: PAUL QUINN
items.text: Well, he wants to be the TMO. He wants to watch the video.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: Wants to be the video ref.

items.speaker: PAUL QUINN
items.text: He wants to be the video ref—the TMO—but he is also a bit
worried about making sure he gets the corporate hospitality. What he does not know is
that he is, I think, off the list for corporate hospitality, because people do not want to
host people who watch bad movies.
Let me finish by mentioning Sue Moroney.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member’s time has expired.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: The speech made by the member who has just
resumed his seat, Paul Quinn, is evidence that the Government is clearly struggling. Not
only has it put up Paul Quinn for the general debate but it is talking about a personal
vote and how the Opposition voted on a personal vote. The Government is clearly
struggling, and that was evidenced by Paul Quinn, who suffers from being two inches
shorter that he needed to be to become an All Black, according to the rugby fraternity.
But I think that sad speech he made is just more evidence that he is suffering from short
man’s legacy.
I want to focus on the poll that is coming up, and we will see whether the
Government is struggling. I refer to the poll that is about to happen in Mana. We know
that it will be a poll on the Government’s policies. It has to be, because Hekia Parata
said she does not do second place. So if she comes second in that by-election, it must be
a commentary on the Government’s policies. John Key knows this.

items.speaker: Hekia Parata
items.text: It’s a highly aspirational electorate that’s been held for 60 years by a
low-ambition Government.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: She is very loud here in the House, but we will see how she gets
on in the electorate.
John Key knows that the Mana by-election will be about the Government’s policies.
The New Zealand Herald of 24 September said we should not blame him for chasing
10 Nov 2010 General Debate 15175
every potential voter in Porirua and Whitby. Then it went on to state: “It was
reminiscent of a scene in The Simpsons movie where the US Government, having lost
its credibility, gets super-nice-guy and actor Tom Hanks to announce the destruction of
the town of Springfield while gently rustling a boy’s hair.” That is what the New
Zealand Herald had to say about John Key and his campaign style, out in the electorate
of Mana.
Of course, John Key has gone to a few early childhood education centres. He was
very brave to do that, because we all know that the National Government has cut
funding to early childhood education, thereby increasing costs to families and making it
extremely difficult for the parents of Mana to have their children participating in early
childhood education. John Key visited Mana Montessori, a centre that has 60 children,
and, yes, the quality of education for those children is in doubt because it is one of the
centres where funding has been cut by John Key. He cut the funding in the Budget, then
he visited the early childhood centres and stroked a small boy’s hair, just like Tom
Hanks in The Simpsons. But it did not work very well. The school head, Nicola Dickie,
said she wished there had been no funding cuts to early childhood education and that the
school was likely to introduce a fee increase for parents. What will that do for the young
children of Mana and their future? We know that families really struggle when fees go
up.
What about First Five Community Childhood Centre? I do not know whether Hekia
Parata has been there, but I know that Kris Fa’afoi has. He is an excellent candidate for
Labour, and he has been to visit the centre. That centre has 34 children, and it will also
face a funding cut. In May, its treasurer, David Conwell, said there was no choice but to
increase fees for care over the 20 hours scheme. He said that parents using that centre
would be facing increases of $40 to $50 per week per child. He said that the parents
were shocked but they understood.
One of the parents actually knows about this because she is also on the management
committee, and her name is Niki Alefosio. She has two children at the centre, and she
knows that she now has to find $100 extra per week to keep sending her two children to
that centre. She is part of the centre’s cooperative management group, and says that if
she takes into account other factors like rising GST—another National Government
policy—she is looking at an extra $10 per day per child. She says she may need to look
at cutting back on family outings or savings. That is the sort of impact that this
Government’s policies are having on the families of Mana. Mrs Alefosio works 30
hours a week, but she said part-time work may not now be viable. She said she may
now need to look at going to full-time work or looking at another form of childcare, just
to make ends meet.
Then there is Jane Wild, who also has two children at the same centre. She said that
the funding cuts were “really stink”—that is what she had to say about it. Her son Max
receives 20 free hours of childcare and she pays for an extra 4 hours. She also has a 1-
year-old by the name of Cameron, and he goes to that centre for 16 hours. She will have
to pay extra for him. That is the effect of the Government’s policies in Mana.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: We have just heard
from my parliamentary colleague Sue Moroney. Yet again she concentrated on Mana. It
seems to me that Labour members are concerned about Mana, and indeed they should
be. If they do not get more than their current majority, then it says a lot about Labour.
It seems that Labour cannot even run its own caucus; I dread to think how it would
try to run the country. [Interruption] Yes, it really does pose questions. One need look
only at the votes last night to see that Labour is at sixes and sevens as a party.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Six and 17.
15176 General Debate 10 Nov 2010

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Yes, six and 17. On a matter of national significance, a
bill that ascertains how we are seen internationally, Labour splits its vote. It seems it is
as divided on this matter as it is on the party leadership. The Labour Party cast 23 votes
in favour and 11 votes against, and four abstentions—abstentions. These members of
Parliament are paid to make decisions, not to sit on the proverbial fence, twiddling their
thumbs, leaving the hard thinking to the rest of Parliament. If they abstain on this one,
one wonders what else they might abstain on.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. There have been
previous Speakers’ rulings about tedious repetition. There is tedious repetition from one
speech to another. Maybe they should just table the research unit notes.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: We will not have any further points of order on this. The member
should not interrupt the member’s speech like that; that is not fair.

items.speaker: Hon John Carter
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I am sorry to interrupt. There
have also been Speakers’ rulings about idiot interruptions through points of order. The
member should be brought to order; it is not good enough.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I do not know where the member has been for lunch, but it is not
hard to see that I am on my feet. He will be silent. Points of order should not be used to
call a member what that member just called him; I will not repeat it. I have already
reprimanded the Hon Trevor Mallard for frivolously interrupting a member’s speech. At
least it was in moderate humour and it was not nasty. The member raised this point of
order in quite a nasty way, and that is not helpful. I go back to the first point that
members should not interrupt, especially in the general debate.

items.speaker: Hon John Carter
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I am quite embarrassed by
the comment you made about my lunch. It was quite inappropriate, actually. For lunch,
I was not very well and I had a piece of chicken, if that is of any use to the House.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member will resume his seat immediately. If the member was
not aware what he said, I say that he called another member of this House an idiot under
a point of order. That is totally unacceptable. He continued to interject when I was on
my feet. He will not do that.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Thinking of the point of order that was raised by the Hon
Trevor Mallard, it is interesting that he talked about repetition. Goodness me! After
wondering who the shadow Leader of the House is, one has to wonder at the repetition
of his points of order—it is all the time, and it goes on.
Let us come back to the point that I know minds are seized with, and that is the fact
that the country cannot afford to be mired in the sort of prevarication that Labour
members have been. In military parlance, yesterday’s performance by Labour can be
seen as the “Charge of the Labour Extremely Light Brigade”. Those members not only
charged in the wrong direction—the wrong way—but they went in all directions at
once. My parliamentary colleague Mr Damien O’Connor—back in the saddle, I am
told—leapt on to the horse and went in completely the wrong direction altogether. To
top it all off, we had a number of desertions from the ranks.
On a slightly more serious note, why do Labour members hate success? They hate
success. It seems that everything that might benefit New Zealand, such as The Hobbit
and the cycleways, Labour is dead against—dead against—and it will do everything it
can to vote against it. Is Labour seriously trying? Is this perhaps a cunning Labour plot
to seriously damage New Zealand’s tourism potential? We in National fortunately are
more focused and we are working hard on the real issues that affect New Zealanders on
a daily basis. The National-led Government has maintained a clear and unrelenting
focus on employment in the midst of a recession.
I was very taken by the very beginning of the Prime Minister’s statement, which
stated that we would protect the entitlements of beneficiaries. We have done that. When
10 Nov 2010 General Debate 15177
we have made changes to the cost of living, when we have made changes to GST, we
have compensated for that. I do not remember Labour engaging in any such activities.
Let us go through a list of the things we have done. We have a growth-enhancing tax
system and we have better, smarter public services. With respect, the resolution of the
neurosurgical questions in Dunedin came to me as a surprise during question time. I
think the answer was fully deserving—fully deserving—of strong and sustained
spontaneous applause, because that is what it merited. We are lifting education, we are
lifting skills, and no matter how rude Labour might be towards our Minister of
Education, she is doing a great job. We are boosting productive infrastructure, we are
pursuing an ambitious trade agenda, and I say well done to Mr Tim Groser for his
efforts in that direction. We are cutting red tape and regulations.
To conclude on the matter of cutting red tape and improving regulations, I have been
going around a number of councils lately. We did not just reduce the number of
complaints about the Resource Management Act; we stopped them altogether.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Kia
ora tātou katoa me huri te kei o te waka ki wāhi kē. Kua waimarie te Pāti Māori i ēnei
marama. Tuatahi, nā mātou te take o te kai hikareti i kōkiri ki mua i te Komiti Take
Māori, ā, kātahi anō taua pūrongo ka puta. Kua oti i a Tariana Turia te whai ake i ētahi
wāhanga o tērā pūrongo hei whakatinana i ōna kōrero. Koi rā te pai o te noho tūranga ā-
Minita nei.
Nōnātatanei i puta te pūrongo o te Kōmihana ā-Ture mō te waipiro. Arā nō ōna
kōrero mō te tau e tika ana kia taea ai e te hunga taiohi te hoko waipiro, unu rānei i te
waipiro, ko te rāhui tonu i ētahi inu i te tirohanga kanohi, ērā take katoa.
Ko te mea tuatoru, ko te pire whakakore mihini ā-petipeti i raro i tōku ingoa. He mea
tēnei i puta nā runga i te tokomaha o te iwi Māori e whai ana i tēnei momo āhuatanga. I
tōku kāinga tonu i Rotorua, i a au e haere ana ki te taunga waka rererangi ki te haere mai
ki Pōneke nei mā te waka kawe, i kaha kōrero mai ngā kaitaraiwa mō ō rātou kitenga,
ko te āhuatanga o te hunga whakapau moni nā ngā mahi petipeti. Kua kite tonu au i te
kino kua puta mai mō tētahi whānau nā tēnei mahi kino. Nō reira e tika ana kia whai te
Pāti Māori i ēnei take.
Ko tōna tikanga, ka tae taku pire gambling harm reduction ki mua i te aroaro o te
Whare Pāremata ā ngā rā ta ta kei mua i te aroaro. Ko te āhua nei ka aro mai ētahi o te
Whare ki te tikanga o tēnei pire. Pēnei i a au nei, kua kite tātou i te kino o ngā mīhini
nei. Ehara i te mea kei te kī au, kārekau he painga e puta mai ana nā ngā mīhini, kāo!
Kei te mōhio tonu tātou he moni te painga. He moni e tukuna atu ai ki ngā rōpū, ngā
tīma hākinakina hei āwhina i a rātou pea ki te hoko kākahu. He moni āwhina i ngā
marae, he aha atu, he aha atu. Ko tā mātou kī e pēnei ana, he kino ake te kino i te pai.
Koi nei te mea ohorere ki a au, ko ngā rōpū pēnei i a Problem Gambling, Poverty
Action Waikato, Salvation Army, Family First. Ko Len Brown tonu te tumuaki hou o
Tāmaki-makau-rau kua kaha tautoko mai i te wairua o tēnei pire. Ko ētahi o ngā mema
o te Rōpū Nāhinara tonu kua kī mai ki a au, kei te tautoko rātou i te tikanga o tēnei pire.
He pōti ā-wairua tēnei, me kī he conscience vote. Arā, mā te wairua o te mema ia e
tohu, āe ranei me tautoko, kāre rānei. Ko te mate kē, ko te āhua nei kei te herea te kakī o
ngā mema o te Nāhinara, o ACT tonu, ā, ka whai rātou ko te kōrero o tō rātou wepu. He
aha i pēnei ai, mēnā kei te mōhio tonu te nuinga o te Whare, he take kei konei? He take
ki te hunga pōhara, ki ngā Māori me Ngāti Pasifika, he take e pā ana ki te hunga hoko
mīhini ki ngā pāpara kāuta e tuku koha, mēnā ka whakawātea mai ngā kaihoko waipiro i
ngā kūaha ki wā rātou mīhini. He take kei konei i te mea, ko te moni ka puta mai i
Rotorua, ka whakapauhia kētia ki wāhi kē. He take kei konei i te mea, ko ētahi o ngā
moni o ngā mīhini ka haere ki ngā karapu whakaomaoma hōiho hei moni tuku. Ko ēnei
kōrero katoa, kāore e kore, ka puta hei te pānuitanga tuatahi ā kō ake nei engari ko tāku
15178 General Debate 10 Nov 2010
kē, he āki i ngā rōpu katoa kia kaua e here i wā rātou mema mō tēnei take. He pōti ā-
wairua tēnei, waiho mā te wairua o tēnā, o tēnā e tohu.
Koi nei ngā akoranga o te noho i te Whare Pāremata. Tuatahi, mēnā kei a koe te
minitatanga ka taea te whakatinana i ngā kaupapa here o tō rōpū. Tuarua, ahakoa pēhea,
ahakoa ko te wawata me te ngākaunui, me whai hoa koe, tō rōpū rānei kia eke ki te ono
tekau mā rua o ngā pōti, arā, kia toa tō pōti. Ki te kore, he moumou tāima te kōrero. Ka
toru, me noho hei Kāwanatanga. Ki te kore e noho hei Kāwanatanga, ko tāu he pāinaina
i te rā, he moemoeā te mahi, he whiuwhiu kōhatu te mahi. Koinei te āhuatanga o Reipa i
tēnei wā, e kore e taea te aha. He kōrero noa iho te mahi, ā, karekau he whiwhinga.
Koinei te āhua o ngā kōrero e rere haere nei i tēnei wā i te Ao Māori, arā, mō te pire
hou mō te takutai moana. I kī ake te Pāti Māori ka ūkuia katoatia te pire takutai moana
nā te mea, he mea muru taua pire. Ka rua, ka whakatuwherahia ngā kūaha ki ngā
huarahi katoa, kua mutu? Aroha mai. Nō reira, kua ea te wāhi ki a mātou o te Pāti
Māori.
[Thank you, Mr Speaker. Greetings, one and all. Allow me to set the stern of the
canoe in another direction. The Māori Party has been fortunate in recent months.
Firstly, we brought the issue of cigarette smoking before the Māori Affairs Committee,
which has just released its report. Tariana Turia has begun implementing some aspects
of the report. That is one of the good things about being a Minister of the Crown.
The Law Commission recently released its review on alcohol. Among other things, it
recommends a minimum purchase and consumption age for youths, and a total ban on
some drinks.
Thirdly, there is the Gambling (Gambling Harm Reduction) Amendment Bill, under
my name. It emerged because of the large number of Māori people involved in this sort
of thing. It is very prevalent in my town of Rotorua. When I have been on my way to the
airport to catch a flight to Wellington, taxi drivers have spoken at length about what
they have seen and how people spend their money on gambling. I have seen for myself
the terrible effects that some families experience as a consequence of this terrible
addiction to gambling. So it is only right that the Māori Party address issues like these.
According to procedure, my Gambling (Gambling Harm Reduction) Amendment Bill
should come before the House soon. Interest in the purpose of this bill is apparent from
some members of the House. They, like me, see the evil side of these gambling
machines. It is not as though I am saying that these machines have no benefits at all.
Far from it! We are absolutely sure that revenue accrues. Organisations receive grants,
sports teams get assistance to purchase uniforms, marae receive financial help, and so
on, and so on. But what we are saying is that negatives far outweigh positives.
Organisations like Problem Gambling, Poverty Action Waikato, the Salvation Army,
and Family First New Zealand are a surprise to me. The new mayor for all of Auckland,
Len Brown, is a strong supporter of the spirit of this bill. Some National members have
told me they support the purpose of this bill. This is a spiritual or conscience vote. The
conscience of each member will determine whether they vote yes or no. The problem is
that it seems that members of both National and ACT are tied by the neck to follow what
their whip demands. Why did it come to this, if most members of this House realise that
there is an issue here? It is an issue for those on lower incomes, for Māori and Pasifika
people. There is an issue here that relates to those who sell gambling machines to pubs,
and who make donations if alcohol vendors make their gambling machines available at
the door. There is an issue here because some of the revenue that comes from Rotorua
is being spent somewhere else; some of the money from the machines is going to the
horse racing industry as grants. All of these points will no doubt soon emerge at the
first reading, but I really urge all parties not to force their members to vote along party
lines. This is a conscience vote. Let each member make up their own mind.
10 Nov 2010 General Debate 15179
This is what one learns by being a member of Parliament. Firstly, if one has a
portfolio, one is better placed to implement party policies. Secondly, regardless of
personal desire and commitment, a member must have an alliance, or their side must
receive 62 of the votes to ensure their vote finishes at the top. If this is not achieved,
talking becomes a waste of time. Thirdly, one must be in Government to be effective
here, otherwise all one can do is lie in the sun, dream on, and cast stones about. That is
Labour’s current position: merely talking and getting no rewards.
This is the current situation in Māoridom, with all the commentary flying about over
the new foreshore and seabed bill. The Māori Party stated that it would repeal the
foreshore and seabed Act totally, because it is confiscating legislation. Secondly, the
new legislation opens up doors to every avenue. Is that it for me? I am sorry. So that is
it from us, the Māori Party.]
SU’A WILLIAM SIO (Labour—Māngere): Mr Speaker, talofa lava, and to
members of this House I am grateful for the opportunity to also make a contribution to
this debate. In the past several weeks, perhaps the past three general debates, we have
listened to the members of the John Key Government talk about Mana. All of a sudden
today they are no longer talking about Mana but are trying to make a big ado about
nothing. Yet, in those past several weeks, I have sat and listened to members of the John
Key Government keep repeating how good and wonderful they were to the people of

items.speaker: Mana. That reminded me of an old saying
items.text: “Na’o le moa sope lava e toe vivi’i e ia lava
ia.”
I will translate that saying for my friend across the room, Tau Henare, whose
Samoan is not as good as mine. It says: “The cock is the only bird that crows its own
praises.” For the past three or so general debates that was all we heard from the National
Government members—praising how good they were towards the people of Mana.
It is important that the people of Mana know that the success or failure of this John
Key Government, and its policies, can be measured by how the Government treats the
people in communities like Mana. The Mana electorate is diverse in its peoples,
cultures, languages, and faiths. Mana is a microcosm of New Zealand society now and
into the future, so the way the John Key Government treats the Mana community
enables us to see how it would treat the rest of the nation. We have to ask, and I hope
the people of Mana continue to ask this Government between now and 20 November,
how the Government treats the people of the diverse communities of Mana.
I say with the greatest of respect, this John Key Government has treated Mana in the
same way that we saw John Banks treat South Auckland not long ago. This Government
treats the people of Mana in the same way that John Key treated South Auckland; he
treated it with disdain and disrespect. I have to add that he was aided and abetted by the
John Key Government.
I give some examples of how the people of Mana have been affected by the John
Key Government and its policies. In June this year we read in the Kapi-Mana News:
“More than 2,000 Mana children will be affected by Budget cuts to early childhood
education and the people of Mana, their families, have every right to feel betrayed by
this Government.” Information obtained by Labour from the Ministry of Education
shows that 2,109 children are enrolled at 47 early childhood education services in the
Mana electorate. Those services currently receive funding because they have 80 to 100
percent qualified staff. The John Key Government will cut that funding from next
February, leaving a shortfall of $25 per child per week. Early childhood centres will
likely pass that cost on to parents or sacrifice the quality of education those children are
receiving. Local families have every right to feel betrayed by this Government, which
broke its promise to keep existing early childhood education subsidies in place. When I
visit groups, churches, and community organisations in parts of Mana I hear parents
15180 General Debate 10 Nov 2010
express their concern about the future of their young children. They express that
concern because not only is this Government cutting the valuable funding that goes into
the education of those children—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman
items.text: Not true.
SU’A WILLIAM SIO: It is very true.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman
items.text: Not true.
SU’A WILLIAM SIO: I tell the Minister to read what is written in the Kapi-Mana
News. The Minister’s comment is another example of somebody who sits in an ivory
tower so does not know the pain and struggles that the people of Mana are going
through. I tell him that Kris Fa’afoi knows what is going on.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Who?
SU’A WILLIAM SIO: Kris Fa’afoi.

items.speaker: HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Tēnā koe e te Mana Whakawā, me te Whare. I am
delighted to stand as the National list MP based in Mana and to have the opportunity of
my parliamentary role to congratulate Porirua on winning three Gold Awards at the
International Awards for Liveable Communities, held in Chicago last night. Porirua
achieved gold for its Village Planning Programme, winning first place in the socio-
economic section of the Environmentally Sustainable Project Award. It also won a Gold
Award in topping the community sustainability criteria in the Whole of City Award.
That is particularly important because they competed against 43 other cities from
around the world, included in which were Montreal, Vancouver, and Beijing.
The reason I start my contribution with that today is that if we listen to the
Opposition, the only thing we would hear about the Mana electorate would be doom and
gloom. The people there want the full story of all the communities of Mana told to the
world, because they are proud of what they are achieving every day. Unfortunately, the
attitude of members opposite was personified and typified by their vote on the Rugby
World Cup 2010 (Empowering) Bill last night; they try to ride all sides of a story—they
are for, they are against, they do not know, they are ambivalent, and they are
ambiguous. That they are in disarray is the fact of the matter.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: A casserole?

items.speaker: HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I thank Mr Calder. They are a verdant casserole of complexities
in disarray.
The fact is Mana has a great story to tell across the board. The crime rate in the
Kapiti-Mana Police District is the lowest in the Wellington region. In terms of health, I
am sure the House was delighted to hear—although it could be forgiven for thinking
otherwise, because of the acrimonious remarks thrown by members opposite—the
Minister of Health yesterday advise the House that in the 2 years of this National
Government the number of elective surgery procedures has climbed 57 percent in the
Mana electorate.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Hear, hear!

items.speaker: HEKIA PARATA
items.text: It climbed by 57 percent. As for outpatient consults, they have
climbed 30 percent.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: So what!

items.speaker: HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I will tell Mr Mallard so what. For 60 years the Labour Party has
had—apparently—a safe seat in Mana, and what does it have to show for it? A legacy
of poor health, a legacy of deferred maintenance in housing, a legacy of people who are
undereducated.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: So what!

items.speaker: HEKIA PARATA
items.text: So what! I and the National Party care about making a
difference for the people of Mana. We care about backing the people of Mana into
business. We care about the Porirua youth, of whom there are a significant number, as
10 Nov 2010 General Debate 15181
witnessed by the Porirua Youth Awards, which were held last week. This party in
Government wants to celebrate achievement. Yes, there are problems; yes, we must
address them, and are we? Yes, we are. This record in health demonstrates that.
I have been criticised by the Opposition for apparently remaining silent on roading. I
am not silent on roading; I absolutely support this Government’s decision to invest $2.2
billion—by the way, our scheme has been costed, unlike the Opposition’s scheme—in a
corridor from Wellington Airport to Levin. I have spent my time advocating that the
impact be as minimal as possible, that the schools be as little affected as possible, that
the focus on environmental screening be important, and that the interchange options be
the best possible available.

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: Where are the plans?

items.speaker: HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Unlike Mr Hughes, I do not think public silence means total
silence, because effectiveness does not require press releases every 5 minutes that say or
mean nothing. My interest is in how we get the best possible outcome for all the
communities of Mana. It is a young population, it is multicultural, and it is aspirational.
I want more for the families, the kids, and all of those communities. Unlike Labour,
which has had 60 years to do something about it, I in 3 years have made significant
differences, and I can point to them. This Government can point to them, because what
we are interested in is—

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: How sweet is the kūmara?

items.speaker: HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Yes, quite right, Opposition members also specialise in cultural
insults, which they put other people up to talk about.
Our Government is interested in sustainable economics. It is interested in sustainable
health, which is why we have seen an improvement. It is interested in sustainable
policing, which is why we have seen a decline in the crime rate. It is interested in
sustainable employment, which is why we have seen an improvement—yes, it is modest
but it is an improvement nevertheless—in employment. That is what this Government
stands for. Kia ora.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Kris Fa’afoi’s chances of winning the
Mana by-election just went up even further. Every time Hekia Parata stands up in
Parliament, or shifts so that she is sitting behind somebody who is speaking, Kris
Fa’afoi’s chances of winning the Mana by-election go up just a little bit further. The
people in Mana, like the rest of New Zealand, know that they were sold a lemon at the
2008 general election. All of the promises that National made are being broken right,
left, and centre; it had no intention of keeping them. Hekia Parata thinks that if she just
screams a little bit louder about how proud she is of all the promises that National has
broken, then somehow the people of Mana will be gullible enough to vote for her and
put her in as their member of Parliament. They are not as gullible as that; they are not as
stupid as that. They know that National has not delivered what it promised. They know
that they are not better off under National.
There is no ambition for the people of Porirua under this National Government. Phil
Heatley wants to take away their houses. The old people in Porirua who have lived in
those State houses and who have raised their families in those State houses will have
them taken away by Phil Heatley. They will have their houses taken away from them. I
say to Phil Heatley that they are not just houses; they are homes. People have lived in
those homes for many years, they have raised their kids there, they have neighbours
whom they have known for most of their lives, and their kids have gone to the local
school. It is not just a house; it is a home. I think it is absolutely disgraceful that Phil
Heatley thinks that it is acceptable to throw them out of the houses that they have lived
in for all that time. Hekia Parata has said nothing. She has said absolutely nothing about
15182 General Debate 10 Nov 2010
Phil Heatley’s plan to throw State housing tenants out of their homes because he wants
to give them to somebody else.
Phil Heatley claimed that the previous Labour Government was a slum landlord.
What has he done since he became the Minister of Housing? He has cut funding. He has
cut funding for maintaining State housing since he became the Minister. I bet very little
money is going into redeveloping State houses in Porirua, just as very little money is
going into redeveloping State houses in my electorate just across the hill in Rimutaka.
In fact, National has abandoned a whole lot of State houses. The houses are now in such
bad nick it will not put tenants in them. Instead of doing them up, it has just abandoned
them altogether. It is leaving them completely empty. That is what this Government
thinks is the priority in housing: turf people out of their houses, turf them out of their
homes, and then leave the houses empty. That is this Government’s housing strategy
and it is an absolute disgrace.
The people in Mana will know. They will pass judgment on this Government in
another 2½ weeks, and the judgment will be clear. They have had a gutsful of the
broken promises. They have had a gutsful of being told that they were going to get a
Government that was ambitious for New Zealand. It was going to turbocharge the
economy. Do members remember that? National was going to turbocharge the
economy. What has happened instead? Unemployment has gone up. Bill English called
the unemployed collateral damage. That is what Bill English thinks about the people
who have lost their jobs. Those people are National’s collateral damage. National does
not care about the people who have lost their jobs because of its bad managing of the
economy.
It does not care about the people who feel betrayed that it broke its promise not to
increase GST. What did John Key say? He said that if National did a halfway decent job
of managing the economy it would not need to increase GST. Either John Key was not
telling the truth, or he has admitted that National has done an appalling job of managing
the economy. He said that if National did a good job of managing the economy, GST
would not go up. GST has already gone up. Less than 2 years after National became the
Government, it put up GST. It is another broken promise to add to the long list.
National said it would not cut education funding. It should tell that to the parents in
my electorate who send their kids to kindergarten, because the Rimutaka Kindergarten
Association has lost $1 million in funding. It has lost $1 million in funding at the hands
of a Government that said it would not cut funding for early childhood education. That
is exactly what it has done.
Across the board the communities are feeling the pinch. They are feeling the effect of
the Government’s funding cuts. Our elderly are struggling to make ends meet because
of the rising cost of living. What does the National Government do? It cuts their home
help hours. It cuts their home help hours, which will ultimately lead to more old people
ending up in hospital. It is a Government that is already out of touch with ordinary
working New Zealanders like the people who live in the Porirua Basin in Mana. This
Government is out of touch.

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: I guess it is up to the Government member
for the electorate of Kaikōura to have the last word, and I have to say that the Rugby
World Cup 2011 (Empowering) Bill was the winner on the day. When we stop to look
at it, we see that it truly paints Labour in the colours that it stands for. It is red-faced, it
is all over the show, and it is not presenting a unified face. At a time when it should be
unified and focused on the challenges ahead, it is divided into factions, and it is
dysfunctional. When we stop to look at Labour in that light, we see its true colours.
Let us have a look at Labour when it was in Government. It is very good to see what
actually happened in the dying days of that reckless, overspending Labour Government.
10 Nov 2010 General Debate 15183
One of its leading bills was the Electoral Finance Bill. What was its aim? It was to
divide and rule. It was to control. When we look at the way it was responded to we see
that it really wound up the people of New Zealand. What did the foreshore and seabed
legislation do? It divided New Zealand. Again, Labour was going to divide and rule.
What we are seeing today around the Rugby World Cup bill is no different from what
we saw in the dying days of that Labour administration.
So what are we seeing today? We are seeing exactly the same thing. Let us reflect on
it. Earlier in the year we had that bus driving around the country. It was painted red and
had the words “Axe the Tax” on it. What was Labour going to do?

items.speaker: Hon Maurice Williamson
items.text: The blunderbuss!

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: Yes, it blew up in Labour members’ faces. They are now in a cleft
stick, in the sense that within their own numbers they cannot actually make a policy
decision. Again they are divided.
A couple of weeks back we had the unbelievable audacity of Labour doing the work
of the unions. It was doing the bidding of the unions and working against the economic
best interests of New Zealand. It backed the unions and backed the Australian initiative
to create chaos and mayhem in our remarkable film industry. When we look at the track
record we see nothing but chaos and confusion around Labour. I believe that that is a
strategy Phil Goff is employing to maintain the leadership. Obviously, the state of
confusion is the key to his leadership and his survival.
So what conclusion do we come to? When there is a lack of leadership there is
confusion. I and other members on this side of the House in Government say that New
Zealand deserves better. Two years ago the people of New Zealand made the best
choice of their lives and that was between two very stark contrasts: a focused, grounded
National Government and a confused and dysfunctional split Labour Opposition.
Let us talk about the positive things that the Government is doing. I may run out of
time in doing so. We are building a brighter future for all New Zealanders, which is
very important. We are rebalancing the economy, with 75 percent of New Zealanders
paying 17.5 percent tax. The Budget will deliver, over 4 years, 170,000 jobs and an
increase in wages of $7,000. In health we are transferring as much as is possible of
taxpayers’ dollars to the front line to deliver better medical outcomes for New Zealand.
And, of course, the main policy in education is improving plain-language reporting to
parents in order to improve achievement in literacy, writing, and numeracy for our
children, which are musts in a modern economy.
Then we have the incredible efforts and strategy in infrastructure. The wisdom of this
Government to put commissioners into Environment Canterbury will show a very good
dividend for this country’s economy going forward. The Canterbury Water
Management Strategy is an amazing strategy. It took backbone, courage, and clarity of
leadership. In the research and development field, the 2010 Budget provided science
and innovation grants and vouchers that will certainly help our businesses to compete
globally. Our free-trade agreements are working very well, and we are looking forward
to the Trans-Pacific Partnership coming to fruition. Of course, there are modifications to
the Resource Management Act and business compliance to make sure that businesses
can survive.
New Zealanders can have confidence that they are in good hands. The Government is
doing a fantastic job. We are aware today that Labour is totally dysfunctional.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.

items.speaker: Hon LIANNE DALZIEL
items.text: I would like to invite the
member Paul Quinn to take the opportunity of what is, I think, his first time in the chair
to answer some questions, because that is really his role as the member in charge of the
Electoral (Disqualification of Sentenced Prisoners) Amendment Bill.
The first question I have—because I could not get the answer to this question at any
stage during this entire debate and I do not think my colleagues could get the answer to
this question from the select committee hearings they had, either—is how many people
voted in the 2008 election while they were in prison. I want to know how many
prisoners actually voted in the 2008 election. The reason I want to know the answer to
that question is this: when one designs legislation, one obviously has a mischief that one
is seeking to remedy. Everyone knows that one of the basic rules of interpretation is that
judges will always go back and ask what the mischief was that the legislation was
designed to remedy. In looking at the mischief that this was designed to remedy, we
look at the provisions of the bill. The provisions state very clearly that the legislation
prevents people from going on to the electoral roll—in fact, they are disqualified from
being on the electoral roll—if they are serving a sentence of imprisonment. They cannot
register as an elector, and that is the technique that has been used. It is probably,
obviously, because a specific number of people have taken up their duty to vote in a
general election while they have been in prison, and I want to know how many did that.
How many did that in the 2008 election? I could ask for previous years’ elections
figures, but I am asking the member in charge of this bill to tell us how many
prisoners—how many people in prison—on the day of the last general election actually
recorded a vote. That is my first question.
Then I would like the member to address—once he has addressed the question of
how many prisoners voted—some of the anomalies that have arisen as a result of how
his bill will apply. I ask the Committee to remember that it is the disqualification of the
person from registering as an elector that prevents them from voting on the day. It does
not say that one cannot actually vote; it just says that one cannot register as an elector.
Someone has to come off the electoral roll. That is quite an interesting thing to do for
somebody who is in prison for, say, a 4-year period. It means that they will be
disqualified from registering as an elector, so they will have to come off the electoral
roll when they go into prison. But what if they come out of prison before the general
election is held? If they come out of prison before the general election is held, they will
have to reregister in order to be able to start voting again from that point on. Of course,
they will be legally allowed to vote from that point, because they will be legally
required to register as an elector. I think what the member in charge of this bill has not
10 Nov 2010 Electoral (Disqualification of Prisoners) Amdt Bill 15185
really responded to in any of the debates so far is that it is a legal requirement to be on
the roll, yet he is saying to somebody that because that person has committed a crime,
he or she is no longer legally required to be on the roll. It seems rather ironic to me.
Anyway, the member can perhaps deal with that.
We will have one person released the day before the election and one person released
on the Monday. They have exactly the same sentence for the same crime, but one gets
released the day before the general election and one gets released two days after—as
general elections are always held on a Saturday—so what happens then? Why is one
person treated in a way where they can get on the electoral roll that day? As they leave
the prison gates they will go straight down to the post office and get on the electoral
roll; I am sure they will, will they not? That will be their real incentive for good
behaviour, to get their right back to vote! They will dash down to the local post office
and they will get on to the electoral roll as quickly as they can, so that they can vote the
next day. But the person who is released on the Monday will, sadly, miss out. Why will
we have such an anomalous situation? That is my second question.
My third question goes to the difference between someone who gets a prison
sentence and someone who gets home detention for exactly the same offence. There will
be different criteria applied to each one. I want the member to tell the Committee
whether he has thought this through for people who cannot get home detention, not
because of the nature of their crime but because of the nature of the home that they
would be applying for home detention to. I know a couple of guys in Christchurch,
young men, both convicted of exactly the same offence in different circumstances, but
essentially they got the same sentence. They both applied for home detention. One did
not get home detention; the other one did. I know that members have said it was
because one lived in Fendalton and one was Māori and lived in Aranui but there is more
to that story than meets the eye. The parents of the Fendalton young man were very
ashamed of what he had done. They were backing their son to rehabilitate himself. They
wanted to keep him out of prison at any cost, not only for his future career but also so
he would not mix with people who perhaps would lead him on the wrong path. They
admitted that he had already gone down that way, but they were prepared to provide
him with genuine support, discipline, and love. They were going to ensure that he would
stay on the straight and narrow from there on in. The Aranui kid did not have that, and
that is why he did not get home detention. I do not think our society will do fair justice
to people in his situation until we are prepared to offer him an alternative to prison—the
same that the young man from Fendalton got. I do not disagree at all with the young
man from Fendalton getting home detention; I think it was the right thing to do. But I
think the State owed an obligation to offer something similar, even though it could not
offer this at home, to the young Māori lad from Aranui as well. That is the third
question.
The fourth question is why the member has chosen the mechanism of prohibiting
people in prison from being on the electoral roll. How will they get on the roll in time, if
they are released the day before an election? I question him about the concept of a civic
duty to vote, when we are treating voting here as if it is a privilege. We actually require
people to be on the electoral roll, as I said before; we do not legally require people to
vote, in the way that people are required to vote in Australia. But every time we get up
and speak at public meetings we always say it is a duty—a civic duty—to be engaged in
the political process. So how do we send that message to anyone when we are treating
voting as a privilege?
I imagine that one day someone might ask Paul Quinn what he did when he had a
term in Parliament, and how he left his mark in those 3 years he was here. He would
say: “I stopped people from voting.”, and the reply would come back: “But don’t we
15186 Electoral (Disqualification of Prisoners) Amdt Bill 10 Nov 2010
have a civic duty to vote?”. He would say: “Yes, but they were criminals who were in
jail.” The person would say: “Oh, really serious criminals, like that guy Graeme Burton,
or William Bell?”, and he would say: “No, no, they already couldn’t vote. My bill
stopped people convicted of much less serious offences from voting.” When the person
asks: “Like what?”, he would answer: “Like a bit of tax fraud, or something minor.”
When he gets told that people get home detention for those sorts of things these days, he
would say: “Well, the people on home detention were never covered—you had to have
been in prison on the day of the election.” The person speaking to the member would
say: “Wow, what an achievement that was! I am sure that that made a real difference.”

items.speaker: Paul Quinn would say
items.text: “Well, it was a deterrent, and the reality is that we should not let
people vote who commit crimes.” The question would come back: “So how many
people do you think the bill stopped from offending?”. Paul Quinn would say: “Well,
look, people would say to themselves: ‘If I commit this crime, I’ll end up in jail. OK,
that’s a risk I’m prepared to take.’ But then they might say: ‘Hang on, I might be in jail
on the day of the election. I don’t know whether that’s a risk I’m prepared to take.’ ” I
ask whether members think that will happen. No, I do not think that will happen.
I have a whole stack of other questions in relation to the decision that the member in
charge of the bill made to send the bill to the Law and Order Committee, and to have
Department of Corrections officials advising on this bill, rather than Ministry of Justice
officials.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: Thank you for the opportunity to offer some
comments on the Electoral (Disqualification of Sentenced Prisoners) Amendment Bill.
Committing a citizen to a period of imprisonment is one of a number of sanctions
available to the State to use with those citizens who break the law. Imprisonment is a
sanction that is designed to deter the citizenry from committing a crime, to protect the
public from lawbreakers, to rehabilitate those in prisons, and, of course, to punish,
through loss of liberties, the incarcerated citizen.
Imprisonment is a significant sanction. I doubt that many prisoners would find much
solace in Byron’s lines:
Eternal Spirit of the chainless Mind!
Brightest in dungeons, Liberty! thou art,
Loss of liberty is a terrible travail to most human beings. I ask members of the
Committee to think for a moment of being stuck in a well-appointed hotel room.
Imagine if the door was locked, one did not have any meals of one’s choice, one could
not turn on the television or the Internet, and one could not have any visits from any
mates. It would not be a lot of fun; one is not free, in other words, to associate with
whosoever one wishes, or otherwise exercise liberties that we daily take for granted.
The philosopher Isaiah Berlin referred to the positive conception of liberty; not
freedom from, but freedom to. Imprisonment at Her Majesty’s pleasure involves a loss
of a number of freedoms to. In prison one loses the freedom of movement, of liberty,
and the loss of a number of freedoms to: the freedom to associate, the freedom of
speech, the freedom to communicate freely with phone or Internet, and many other
freedoms to.
I believe the freedom to vote is an integral part of an individual’s liberty, and of an
individual’s freedoms to. The loss of the freedom to vote upon going to prison is
perfectly consistent with the loss of the other aforementioned freedoms to, concomitant
with a term of imprisonment. Let us explore the reality. Many criminals have a long
string of convictions before they receive a prison term. A judge does not sentence a
person to prison lightly in this country. It is a last resort reserved for either the more
serious offenders or repeat offenders.
10 Nov 2010 Electoral (Disqualification of Prisoners) Amdt Bill 15187
This Government is committed to addressing the drivers of crime, and is aiming in
the long term to reduce the size of our prison muster. New Zealand and Australia
currently ban prisoners’ suffrage for prisoners having a sentence of 3 years or more, but
among democratic countries there is no clear policy or threshold at which those
convicted of crimes lose or do not lose their right to vote.
Internationally, we run the whole gamut with regard to prisoners’ suffrage. Some
countries have no disqualification, and even the worst serial offender is allowed to vote.
Some ban voting even after prisoners are released. Others have a total ban on prisoner
voting. There is a continuum; arguments can be made for any number of scenarios about
where along the continuum the threshold for a ban on prisoner suffrage should be. It is
logical, less arbitrary, simple to understand, and entirely consistent with the
concomitant loss of Isaiah Berlin’s freedoms to, which is inherent in any sentence of
imprisonment, for the ban to apply to any prisoner sentenced to prison. I commend this
bill to the Committee.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: That was a fairly good second
reading speech, but I was quite surprised that the member Cam Calder was the one
speaking, rather than the member in charge of the Electoral (Disqualification of
Sentenced Prisoners) Amendment Bill. I think the normal practice at the Committee
stage of a bill, as I think the member should be aware, is that when there is a substantive
Supplementary Order Paper, the member in charge of the bill—normally a Minister, but
in this case Mr Quinn—gets up and explains the substance of that Supplementary Order
Paper. In this case, I think he should have taken responsibility for the situation that led
to the Supplementary Order Paper, which effectively reverses the guts of the bill.
I know that all of us have our first time in the chair. Like the member, I was lucky
enough to be involved in a bill well before my ministerial time.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: A very good bill.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: Well, I do not know if it was very good, actually; it
was legislation on Waikato electricity and gas. As I am indicating to the member, it
would have been better, and it would have been polite to the Committee, if he had stood
up. I think it is fair to say that this will be the highlight of his 3-year parliamentary
career, when people go back and look at the changes that he has made. In the future,
when he is looking out from his home in Roseneath over to the prison on Mount
Crawford, he will be able to say that for a period of time, as a result of his work, there
were people there who could not go on the electoral roll. That will be the peak of his
parliamentary career: he will be able to look out from his house in Roseneath over to
Mount Crawford, and to say that. I do not think he can actually see the prison in the
Hutt Valley from his place; I think he would have to look around the corner a bit from
Roseneath. I know where Rimutaka Prison is and I know where the Hutt Valley is,
unlike Mr Quinn, who is a fairly irregular visitor out there.
In fact, he did not make it to either of the school prize-givings last night. He is the
champion of the valley!

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: Was he up for a prize?

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: The dunce’s prize, because I do not think I have seen
in a bill the time that I have been in Parliament that shows such gross incompetence in
the management of a simple piece of legislation. This is not complicated legislation; it is
relatively simple. I can understand the problems that Maurice Williamson had with his
shipping legislation in the past because it was substantive. I do not really understand
Kate Wilkinson’s problems a couple of weeks ago, as that was simple too. I would have
thought it was impossible to have an effect that is the reverse of the intention of the
member in charge of the bill. I would have thought that a member in charge of
legislation who was even half competent would read it. If he could not understand it,
15188 Electoral (Disqualification of Prisoners) Amdt Bill 10 Nov 2010
then he could get someone to read it too him. If he could not understand it then, he
could get someone with some legal knowledge, such as Simon Bridges—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: No, someone with legal knowledge!

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: To be fair, the junior lawyer from Tauranga has some
legal knowledge—

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: He never won a case.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: Oh no, he could have explained the bill to Paul Quinn.
Then we would not have had Paul Quinn with Supplementary Order Paper 174. That
Supplementary Order Paper can be well summarised as him saying he is sorry. Paul
Quinn in Committee moved an amendment to new clause 6: “To add the following
clause (after line 24 on page 2):”, but really it should say: “I’m sorry”. What the
member has done is almost unforgivable. He sat on a select committee on a bill, he
looked at it carefully, he went line by line through the Supplementary Order Paper, and
he looked at all the changes that were done in the select committee—

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: And then he woke up.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: Well, no, he did not wake up; that is the whole point.
The legislation came to the House wrong because he was asleep. All I want to do is to
congratulate my colleagues on the select committee who let him do it.

items.speaker: PAUL QUINN
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Chairperson. Somewhere in
the Standing Orders I am allowed to, upon resumption of the seat of the previous
speaker, correct a statement of fact. He claimed that I sat on the select committee—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: The member can take a call and do that; I would
need to look up the Standing Order. Does the member want to seek leave to correct it?
What is the member doing? [Interruption] I will take a call.

items.speaker: STUART NASH
items.text: Thank you. It was a difficult decision, I know, but you
came up with the right answer in the end, Mr Chairperson.
When I look at the Electoral (Disqualification of Sentenced Prisoners) Amendment
Bill I wonder if the member Paul Quinn actually spoke to the National Government’s
Minister of Justice—I wonder if he did. When I look at this bill, I see that the only
people who will be in jail for 3 years or less who will vote will be the blokes who voted
for that side of the House, anyway. They are the chaps from the 40-odd finance
companies who, I hope, will end up as guests of Her Majesty in the big house for the
damage they have done to the vast majority of people.

items.speaker: I must say one thing
items.text: the previous National speaker, Cam Calder, spoke about
denying the rights of Kiwis who had done great harm to society. Well, I may be wrong,
but the way I read this bill is that it is only for people who are in jail, or have committed
an offence and are jailed for 3 years or less. The men who have murdered our citizens
and the women who have neglected their children, the ones who are in jail for a long
length of time, have already been denied their right to vote, anyway.
When I look at this bill, I see that this is a nasty bill. What does this bill do? It does
not save any lives, it does not protect society, and it does not deliver equity. There is no
mention of rehabilitation, there is no mention of redemption, and there is no mention of
restoration. It delivers only a further kick in the guts to people in jail who have made
wrong decisions and who are there at the moment for 3 years or less. We will be
denying them every single possible right that they could have. That is the wrong
message to send.
I wonder whether, in fact, the member who is sponsoring this bill took it to caucus to
be debated. The reason I ask is that the Attorney-General himself, who we know knows
absolutely everything about everything, wrote a report that stated that this bill
contravened the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act. The Attorney-General said that. I am
sure the Attorney-General would have been in the caucus when that member brought
10 Nov 2010 Electoral (Disqualification of Prisoners) Amdt Bill 15189
the bill to caucus and said that he wanted to put it in the ballot. I cannot believe that the
Hon Chris Finlayson did not stand up and say “Whoa, hold on a second here. This is not
what our party stands for. This contravenes the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act.”

items.speaker: Simon Bridges
items.text: Whoa!

items.speaker: STUART NASH
items.text: I know that member over there would not have stood for it; he
admitted he lost 50 percent of his cases.
Is this what we want to do? Is this the sort of slippery slope that we want to send our
society down, denying the rights in the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act, a fundamental
piece of constitutional law, which outlines the fundamental rights of every citizen? The
Attorney-General said “No”.
The other thing is that Simon Power stood up in the House—well, he has stood up
numerous times—and said this Government would be hard on criminals. Is this
legislation hard on criminals? He said this Government would look after the rights of
victims. Does this bill attend to the rights of victims? No, it does not. It does not do
anything positive, at all—it does not do anything positive, at all. As my colleague the
Hon Lianne Dalziel asked, will this bill stop people committing crimes? Cam Calder
said it may. Of course it will not. People who commit crimes will not stop and think
“Well, hell, if I go to jail, I’m not going to be allowed to vote.”
This bill has no positive impact whatsoever. It will not stop crime, it will not address
the causes of crime, and it will not address social equity. It does nothing. It does nothing
to help rehabilitate people who are already in jail, and it is not the track that I think our
society needs to go down. I am sure Mr Bridges over there would agree. I cannot
believe that a lawyer who is versed in constitutional law would back any bill that would
deny the rights of citizens and would go against the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act—I
just cannot believe that.
So I ask Mr Quinn to have a look at this bill, to take a deep breath and have a look at
what he is trying to achieve, because I do not know what this bill is trying to achieve.
The worst offenders in our society who have committed the most abhorrent crimes have
been denied the right to vote already—they have been denied the right to vote already.
This bill is aimed at the petty criminal who has a chance of rehabilitation. It is aimed at
the petty criminal who we can provide rehabilitation for. This is not a good bill.

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: The Electoral (Disqualification of
Sentenced Prisoners) Amendment Bill is a worthy bill from a great citizen of New
Zealand, Paul Quinn. What a great citizen of New Zealand! He has done a lot of good
things in his life. Some other members are saying that this will be his finest hour, but I
have a feeling he will get comfortable in that green chair over time. I have a feeling he
might get to sit in it a little bit more in the future. But not only does this man champion
the Hutt Valley—

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: Will the member include him in his Cabinet?

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: If Paul Quinn is in Parliament, he will be in my Cabinet. Not
only does this member champion the valley but in his spare time he is coming up with a
lot of legislation and a lot of ideas, and this is a very good one from that member.
Stuart Nash says this bill is about petty criminals, but I ask him whether it really is
about petty criminals.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: Petty tax fraud, they said before.

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I am sure members opposite say that to people who have been
ripped off by so-called petty tax fraud. It seems to me that one of the central debates
throughout the readings of the bill and, now, in the Committee stage is whether sending
someone to prison is serious enough to take their right to vote from them. Absolutely it
is.
15190 Electoral (Disqualification of Prisoners) Amdt Bill 10 Nov 2010
The last Labour Government, during its several years in office, liberalised the law
and I am not saying I necessarily disagree with that. It introduced a number of
sentences—I think it was seven—that one could get before imprisonment. One can go
through supervision, intensive supervision, electronic bail, and electronic this, that, and
the other thing, before one gets home detention. To be sentenced to imprisonment, a
criminal has to have been convicted of a serious offence. Not only that person’s liberty
but also their right to vote should be denied.
I think Paul Quinn has done a very good thing here. We come back to the question of
principle. Should serving prisoners have the right to vote? That is ultimately what this
comes back to.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: But that’s how it is now. You have to argue why they shouldn’t.

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I ask the member to give me a reason why serving prisoners
should have the right to vote. Give me two or three reasons why they should have the
right to vote.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: No, no, that’s the status quo. You’re the one changing it; you
make the reason.

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Those members do not like it, do they? There is no reason why
serving prisoners should have the right to vote. Those people have landed in the clink
because they have done something serious. They have not stumbled their way into
prison, as Lianne Dalziel or Stuart Nash would have us think. Those people have
systematically committed serious crimes. Under the Sentencing Act the judge has to go
past a number of other sentences before getting to imprisonment. The law says that for
people to be sentenced to imprisonment the judge has to be satisfied that none of those
other sentences are suitable. I ask Labour members to tell me why serving prisoners
should have the right to vote. The only reason I can think of is that Labour wants
prisoners to vote; it thinks that prisoners should have the vote. Why should they? I ask
Labour members to give me some good reasons.
Lianne Dalziel talked about how it was a civic duty to vote. I absolutely disagree
with that. I absolutely disagree that it is a civic duty to vote. That is why I am against,
and have been consistently against, compulsory voting. I do not think people have a
duty to vote. People can opt out of the system if they want to do so and decide not to
vote. Members should not get me wrong; I think people should vote. As a personal
choice, I think people should—

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: Labour’s soft on crime.

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Labour members are soft on crime. They want criminals to
vote. I think people should not opt out. They should take seriously their right to vote,
and they should look at the options, but it is not a duty. Labour members do not like
what I am saying, and it probably is controversial, but I think of council elections and
the plethora of choices people have. Unless a person has gone through and thought
about all of the candidates, does that person have a duty to vote? I do not think so. If
